docs.title: Dynamic dispatch and external code
docs.text: Rule for everything on this page: a call whose target cannot be fixed at compile time is compiled against a declared bound, never against what the implementation happens to do today. Later releases of an implementation may then change freely inside the bound, and a program that compiled keeps being valid.

docs.title: Interface calls
docs.text:
An interface method has a declared effect bound: the widest effect any implementation may have.

  • Default bound: May (Direction). Safe, and cheap because a May call that does not park costs about a call plus a status test (Measured, toy). A bound is written only when the author wants to narrow it, using the same nopark tag as for functions (placeholder syntax; D4).
  • Implementations are checked against the bound when they are compiled. An implementation can be narrower than the bound, never wider. An implementation of a nopark method that calls a May function is a compile error in the implementing module.
  • Callers compile the call against the bound. A caller of a May-bound method uses the suspendable form regardless of the implementation.
  • Vtable entries for May methods hold the f_call/f_resume pair. An implementation that is Never registers a thunk that returns DONE, so the calling code is the same.
  • At link time, if the closed-world call graph shows one reachable implementation, the call may be devirtualised and the thunk and the status test removed. If several implementations exist, the bound still holds; any narrowing is an optimisation of the call site (a switch over known targets), never a change of contract.

This is the answer to "previously valid programs becoming unsafe when implementations change": the check that matters happens in the implementing module against a bound the caller already relied on.

docs.title: Function values and callbacks
docs.text:
A function-typed value (fn(u8[]&): Resp throws Exception) carries a bound the same way. Unannotated, it is May. A value that can be shown Never at the point where it is created (a lambda with no parking calls) can be passed where a May bound is expected. The reverse needs the assertion.

Functions that take function-typed parameters have a conditional summary Cond(P): forEach(list, f) parks iff f may. At a call site where f is statically known, the condition collapses and the call binds to the plain or the suspendable form. At one where it is not, the parameter's declared bound is used.

Callbacks that the runtime invokes (a handler, a timer) are May by contract; the runtime calls the f_call/f_resume pair.

docs.title: Generic functions
docs.text:
Direction: monomorphise (one copy per type argument set, as in C++ and Rust), because it gives each instance exact frame layouts and an exact effect. It needs Tier B IR from the defining module, and instances land in the using module's object (or a link-time instance cache).

A generic function's summary is symbolic in the type arguments: Cond({T}) if it calls a method of T, whose bound comes from the constraint. Resolved at instantiation. The generic body's IR is part of its contract hash, so editing a generic body forces dependants that instantiate it to recompile.

Open (D6): shared generic code with a dictionary, which avoids code growth and makes generics independent of IR retention but costs speed and requires uniform frame layouts for generic locals.

docs.title: Separately compiled libraries
docs.text:
Libraries are compiled modules. Their interfaces are Tier A. The rules in modules cover: contract hash checks at link; widening an effect or layout is breaking; implementations behind interfaces change freely within the bound.

A library that is only available as a native object and header (no .smod) is a foreign library and takes the rules below.

docs.title: Native C interoperability
docs.text:
C declarations carry no ownership or effect information (spec 5.2). A Strata binding must state it:

extern fn crc32(data: u8[]&) -> u32                  // plain: Never. Assumed short and non-blocking.
extern parks fn sleep(d: Duration)                   // existing: a runtime primitive that registers and parks
extern blocking fn pqExec(c: PgConn&, sql: string&) // proposed: may block the OS thread (see below)

An extern fn without a modifier is a promise that it returns quickly and does not block. The compiler cannot verify the promise and nothing in the runtime enforces it. A violation stalls one worker for the length of the call (the same failure mode as a Java thread stuck while pinned); a watchdog may report it (see the table).

extern blocking is the one proposed new keyword in this update (Open; placeholder). It states that the call may block the thread, and is the only way a binding can say so. It carries foreign = blocking and park = May in the summary: the Strata caller sees an ordinary suspending call.

docs.title: Blocking foreign calls
docs.text:
A foreign C function is native stack that cannot be captured, so it cannot be suspended in the middle. Strategies, in order of preference:

Strategy What happens Cost and limits 1. Nonblocking binding (best) Use a readiness/async API of the library (nonblocking sockets, epoll, io_uring); the Strata wrapper calls it and parks on the descriptor. Library must offer it. No extra thread. 2. Offload to a blocking pool (Direction for extern blocking) The call is a park point: the vthread parks, a pool thread runs the call, and a completion wakes the vthread. A thread hop per call (some microseconds); a bounded pool, so a full pool queues work (and that wait is itself a park). Arguments must outlive the park: borrowed arguments must be frame-resident, not on the native stack (same rule as here). Thread-affine libraries need a pinned thread (strategy 3). 3. Dedicated thread A thread owns a library (a connection, a context) and Strata sends it work and awaits replies as messages. Serialises that library's calls; good for thread-affine code. 4. Run on the worker Plain extern fn: the call blocks the worker. Only right for calls that are truly short. Stalls everything on that worker. 5. Compensating worker A monitor notices a worker stuck in foreign code past a threshold and starts another worker so the scheduler keeps a core busy. Does not fix the stuck call. Useful as a backstop and as a diagnostic, not a design.

Recommendation: 1 where available, 2 as the default for anything declared extern blocking, 3 for thread-affine libraries, and a watchdog (diagnostic only, 5's detection without its remedy) for promises broken under 4. All are Open until measured: cost of the thread hop is exactly the kind of figure the evaluation plan must record.

docs.title: Foreign callbacks
docs.text:
C code calls a Strata function (a qsort comparator, a library event callback). The callback runs on whatever native stack C is using.

  • Default (Direction): a callback is compiled as Never (implicitly nopark, so no budget checks). Calling a May function from it is a compile error. Because a callback is invoked from C, it is f_call-only: nothing underneath it can be captured.
  • Exception: callbacks that must park. Declared as parking callbacks, they run on a blocking-pool thread only, under a synchronous driver: the wrapper calls f_call; on PARKED it blocks the OS thread on a wake-up object, and on the wake calls f_resume until DONE. Parking then blocks that thread, not a scheduler worker. This is the block_on of Strata. It is forbidden on scheduler workers (compile error if the call is made from a worker context that is not a pool thread; at minimum, a runtime check).
  • Exceptions cannot cross a C frame. The wrapper catches THROWN and converts it to the library's error convention or aborts. The binding says which.

docs.title: Dynamically loaded modules
docs.text:
Direction: not supported in the first compiler. It must stay possible, so the contract design assumes it:

  • A loadable module is a native shared object plus its .smod interface. At load, the runtime checks: format and ABI versions, imported contract hashes against what is already loaded, and that any interface implementations it registers satisfy the declared bounds.
  • A loaded module can be Never, Cond or May per function like any other; its callers are compiled against bounds, so no reanalysis is needed. This is the benefit of bound-based dispatch.
  • Tension with whole-program optimisation: devirtualisation and fusion assume the set of implementations is closed. A plugin can add implementations. The application's build configuration therefore names the open interfaces (those plugins may implement); calls through them are never devirtualised and keep the thunks. Everything else stays closed-world. The configuration, not new source syntax, carries this (Open, D9).
  • Unloading is out of scope: frames and vtables may point into a module.

docs.title: Compiled modules and application linking
docs.text: A compiled Strata module (working extension .smod; a bundle of them is an archive, .sar) is what a library ships and what an application consumes. It carries enough to type-check, lifetime-check, effect-check and optimise a program against it without the original source. Names and extensions are placeholders.

docs.title: 1. Three tiers of information
docs.text:
The module separates what is needed for correctness from what only enables optimisation. A consumer can drop a higher tier and still get a correct program.

Tier Purpose Contents If absent A: Contract Correctness Exported types and layouts, signatures, borrow origins, effect summaries, interface/dispatch contracts, generic constraints, ownership metadata, versions and hashes The module cannot be used. B: Instantiation IR Correctness for generics and exposed bodies IR of generic functions and types, and of functions the author exposes for inlining Generic code cannot be instantiated downstream. (Unless generics use a shared-code representation; see D6.) C: Optimisation IR Speed and size IR of every non-generic function, call-graph edges with targets, park-point and liveness tables, frame layouts Still correct and linkable through Level-0 entries; no cross-module inlining, devirtualisation or fusion. (cache) Build speed Per-target C and native objects, keyed by hashes Rebuilt on demand.

A module can be shipped as A+B only (a "closed" library: interface and generics, plus precompiled objects) or A+B+C (an "open" one). That is the exact meaning of "without requiring the original source": the compiler needs IR, not text.

docs.title: 2. Contents of a module
docs.text:
header
  magic, format version, ABI version, compiler id
  module name, module version, target triple + layout hash
  content hash, interface hash
imports
  for each imported module: name, version range, and for each symbol used:
    the contract hash that this module was compiled against
exports                                            [Tier A]
  types: layout (or "opaque"), fields visible, cleanup method, copy/move rules,
         whether sync-able (has a lock word)
  functions: signature, per-parameter ownership mode (borrow, consume, Ref),
             borrow origins of the return value, effect summary, throws list
  interfaces: method list, per-method effect bound, vtable layout, versioning rule
  generic definitions: constraints, effect conditions (Cond(P))
  constants and static data a caller may fold
instantiation IR                                   [Tier B]
  IR for generic items and for explicitly inlinable functions
implementation                                     [Tier C]
  typed IR per function, with a per-function content hash
  call-graph edges: direct (symbol), indirect (interface method / function type + its declared bound),
                    address-taken set
  per-function park-point table: state id -> source location, live set, logical function
  frame layout (private) and the Level-0 entry names
  initialisation order and dependencies
debug (optional)
  names, line tables, logical stack maps for fused code
native cache (optional, repeatable)
  per target/compiler/flags: generated C and object, keyed by the inputs below

docs.title: Effect summaries
docs.text:
The summary is part of every exported function's contract, not an attribute of its body:

Summary(f) = {
  park:    Never | May | Cond(P)
  throws:  set of exception types that can escape
  foreign: none | nonblocking | blocking          // reaches a foreign call (see dispatch page)
  yields:  bool                                    // park=May only because of compiler-inserted budget checks; cannot wait on I/O or a lock
}
invariants: cleanup methods are Never; foreign=blocking implies park=May

Cond(P) is stored symbolically, so a downstream module can resolve it with its own arguments. A conditional effect through a type parameter (T.compare that might park) is stored as Cond({T}) and resolved at instantiation.

Summaries are inferred, then exported as part of the contract. The consequence, already noted for borrow origins in spec 5.1: changing an implementation can change the contract with no source signature change. The compiler reports it (versioning).

docs.title: Call-graph information
docs.text:
Retained in Tier C, and also, in reduced form, in the contract:

  • Direct edges: f -> g with the symbol g (module-qualified). Enough for whole-program effect checking and for dead-code elimination.
  • Indirect edges: an interface method or function-typed value, with its declared effect bound. Resolved against known implementations at link time; never assumed resolvable.
  • Address-taken set: functions whose address escapes as a value. Needed to know which functions can be the target of a function-value call.
  • Reachability roots: exported functions, interface implementations, and initialisers.

docs.title: 3. ABI and IR boundaries
docs.text: This is the central design cut: what must stay stable for separately compiled code to link versus what is free to change.

docs.title: Level 0: the stable ABI between modules
docs.text:
Everything a caller compiled against db may rely on, and what db must keep working across releases that claim compatibility:

Item Stable? Symbol name, argument and result passing (C calling convention rules per target) Yes status values DONE/THROWN/PARKED, and the wake reasons including CANCELLED Yes The frame header (resume pointer, state number, parent link, task pointer, result binding) Yes The way a function exposes its two entries (f_call, f_resume) Yes Layout of exported types that are not opaque Yes; changing it is a breaking change Vtable layout of an interface, slot order, per-slot effect bound Yes Exception type identities Yes The frame body (live slots, state numbering, number of frames used) No. Private to the function. Whether the function uses lazy, eager or embedded frames No. The IR No. It is versioned independently; a consumer reads the IR format version.

Keeping the frame body private is what makes incremental compilation work: a caller of db.query never learns how many bytes query's frame is. A callee that changes its locals, adds a park point or switches to eager frames changes nothing a caller's object code depends on. Direction, resting on the lazy convention; if the callee's frame had to be embedded in the caller's, this would not hold (and that is why embedding happens only at link time, from IR, never at module compile).

docs.title: The IR boundary
docs.text:
The IR is what a consumer uses to regenerate code, so it must carry what the generated C needs, and no more:

  • Typed, structured control flow with ownership operations explicit: move, borrow, Ref copy and release, new, cleanup scopes, sync/mutate regions, throw edges.
  • Effects on every call site, and park points marked, so that frame lowering is a function of the IR alone.
  • Not raw source text, comments, formatting or macro structure.
  • Stable under a format version number; the consumer refuses a newer major version.

The minimum IR needed for cross-module optimisation is open (D3).

docs.title: 4. Versioning and compatibility
docs.text:
• Format version (major.minor): the layout of the file. A consumer reads any same-major file.
  • ABI version: the Level-0 rules in the table above. A different ABI means a rebuild, never a silent link.
  • Contract hash, per exported symbol: a hash of exactly its Tier A entry (and for generics and exposed bodies, the Tier B IR). It is the unit of compatibility.
  • Module interface hash: a hash of all contract hashes, for a fast check.
  • Compatibility rule (Direction): an implementation change that alters no contract hash is compatible. A change that narrows an effect (May to Never), reduces throws, or adds an export is backward compatible. A change that widens an effect (Never to May), adds to throws, changes layout or changes a borrow origin is breaking, whether or not the signature text changed.
  • Semantic version policy: breaking contract changes require a major version; the compiler can compare two versions of a module and print the contract diff (which symbols changed and which dimension). This answers spec 10.10 (API stability) at the tooling level; the policy itself is Open.

docs.title: The native cache key
docs.text:
A cached C or object file for a function is valid only for the inputs it was generated from:

key = hash( function IR hash,
            contract hashes of every symbol it references,
            Tier B/C IR hashes of anything inlined into it,
            module ABI + runtime ABI version,
            compiler version, C compiler id + version,
            optimisation level + codegen flags, target triple )

Any input changing gives a different key; a stale entry is never reused, only left to age out.

docs.title: Incremental compilation (default for development)
docs.text:
1. For each module, in dependency order: read the interfaces of imports (Tier A only), type-check, infer effects and borrows, produce IR, lower to Level 0, emit C, cache the object.
  2. Link the objects and the runtime with the system linker. No IR from other modules is read.
  3. Early cut-off: if a module's interface hash is unchanged after recompilation, its dependants are not touched, even though its objects changed (they relink, not recompile).

Correctness across separately compiled modules rests on Tier A plus Level 0. Calls to May functions are compiled to check status because the contract says May, whatever the body does today.

docs.title: Optimised application compilation (release builds)
docs.text:
1. Resolve all modules (names, versions, contract hashes). A mismatch between an importer's recorded hash and the provider's is an error naming the symbol.
  2. Build the closed-world call graph from Tier C edges and the build configuration (entry points, open interfaces).
  3. Check effects across modules with the summaries: a Cond(P) is resolved against real arguments; indirect calls are checked against implementations; a violated bound is an error.
  4. Re-run lifetime/borrow checks that cross modules (only the contracts are needed).
  5. Decide optimisations: devirtualise calls with a single reachable implementation, inline small functions, fuse or embed frame chains, specialise generics.
  6. Re-lower and re-emit only the functions changed by step 5. Everything else keeps its cached Level-0 object.
  7. Run the C compiler and linker; ideally with LTO as an independent layer.

Step 5 is where the retained IR is consumed. If a module lacks Tier C, calls into it stay at Level 0 and nothing else breaks.

docs.title: What each step costs
docs.text:
Cost Why Mitigation Whole-program effect resolution One pass over summaries: proportional to call-graph edges and indirect bound checks Summaries are small and cached per module; independent of code size Devirtualisation and inlining need IR Read and re-lower IR for the functions touched Limit to reachable code from roots; parallel by SCC; cache the results keyed as in section 4 Re-optimisation on change A change to one function can alter fusion decisions upstream Content-hashed products: only chains whose inlined inputs changed are regenerated IR size in the module Tier C is bigger than the contract Tier C is optional; shipped as separate section or file Cache invalidation A wrong key gives wrong code Keys include everything in section 4; unknown dimensions invalidate Cold full build Whole-program mode over all modules Not the default; development uses incremental

These costs are estimated from experience of comparable systems, not measured for Strata. Evaluating the build-time cost is part of the plan.

docs.title: 6. When a module needs recompiling
docs.text:
Recompile module M when any of these changes:

  1. M's own source (or its IR, if only IR is provided).
  2. A contract hash of any symbol M references. Granularity is the symbol, not the whole imported module: M is not rebuilt because an unused export of a dependency changed.
  3. Compiler, runtime ABI, module ABI, C compiler or flag set (the cache key dimensions).
  4. An inlined body, in optimised mode only: if M's cached link-time product inlined or fused a function from N, and that function's Tier B/C IR hash changed.
  5. Build configuration that affects closed-world decisions: the set of open interfaces or the entry points. (Budget checks are language semantics and not a build setting, so they are not a dimension here; the experimental switch that disables them is stamped in the header and refused by normal builds.)

Not a reason to recompile M: a change in an imported function's body that leaves its contract hash alone (in incremental mode); a change in an unreferenced export.

Ripple of effect changes (the main risk). If net.Conn.send becomes May where it was Never, every caller's contract and generated code change, and so does every caller's callers when their own summary widens. The ripple is bounded by the call graph, and stops wherever a nopark tag or an already-May function absorbs it. The module compile prints the contract diff so the cause is visible; this is the same visibility the ownership metadata already needs.

docs.title: 7. Cross-module propagation, example
docs.text:
module net      export Conn.recv       Park=May   foreign=nonblocking    hash n1
                export Conn.close      Park=Never                         hash n2

module db       import net.Conn.recv@n1
                export query           Park=May (via net.Conn.recv)       hash d1
                export escape          Park=Never                         hash d2

module app      import db.query@d1, db.escape@d2
                handle()   -> Park=May      (via db.query)   inferred; nothing written
                render()   -> Park=Never

If db is rewritten internally to cache rows and query now sometimes avoids recv, its body changes but not its contract: d1 is unchanged, app is not recompiled. If db.escape is changed so that it logs through a May function, its summary becomes May, d2 changes, and app is recompiled (and render, if it called escape, becomes May too).

 app.handle ---May---> db.query ---May---> net.Conn.recv   (extern parks)
      |                                     ^ summary read from net.smod
      +--Never--> app.render                ^ no net source needed
 db.smod carries only: query: May; its IR (Tier C) is read in optimised link only

docs.title: Open decisions
docs.text: Each item gives the alternatives, the trade-off and a recommended direction. A recommendation is not a decision: it is what to build first and test.

docs.title: D1. Where continuation lowering happens
docs.text:
• At module compile. Every function is lowered to the Level-0 convention; the module's C and object are final. Pros: fast incremental builds, no IR needed to link, predictable. Cons: no cross-module frame fusion.
  • At application link. Modules ship IR only; lowering runs on the whole program. Pros: best optimisation. Cons: slow links, requires IR from every dependency, weak caching.
  • Both (recommended). Lower at module compile. In optimised mode, re-lower only chains whose inlining or fusion changes them, using retained Tier C IR.

Recommendation: both, with module compile authoritative. Release a first compiler that does only module-level lowering.

docs.title: D2. Borrowed locals and the lazy shape
docs.text:
The lazy strategy copies locals into a frame only on a park, which moves them. A borrow of a moved local dangles. See suspension.

  • Frame-resident borrowed locals; the function uses eager frames (recommended). Correct; loses the lazy saving for functions with borrowed-across-park locals.
  • Pin the local's storage in the task arena. The local is in the arena from the start, not the stack. Cheaper than a full frame; one more arena operation.
  • Forbid borrowing across a park. Simple; too restrictive (recv(buf&)).

Recommendation: the first, then measure how many hot functions it affects. The toy benchmarks did not include this.

docs.title: D3. The minimum IR for cross-module optimisation
docs.text:
Alternatives: (a) full typed IR for all functions; (b) IR for functions under a size threshold and generic ones only; (c) author-marked inlinable functions only.

Recommendation: ship (b) by default as Tier B plus a size-limited Tier C, with the full IR as an option for libraries that want fusion. Measure size against build gain before deciding the default. Minimum requirements on any IR: explicit ownership operations, call-site effects, park points, cleanup scopes, source-independent.

docs.title: D4. Representing effects in public interfaces
docs.text:
Alternatives: (a) infer everything and export it (current plan); (b) require the author to declare the effect of public functions; (c) infer, and let the author optionally assert a bound.

(b) reintroduces colouring. (a) alone lets an implementation change ripple silently through dependants. Recommendation: (c) - an optional nopark tag (the opt-out from budget checks, see suspension 1.1), plus tooling that prints the contract diff between versions, and a version policy that treats widening as breaking. Open: whether the [nopark] attribute form should also replace the existing parks modifier (extern fn[parks]) and extern blocking (extern fn[blocking]) for consistency, and whether to allow parks on non-extern functions as a "may park" promise for stability.

docs.title: D5. Recursion and dynamic dispatch
docs.text: Recursion: SCC fixed point; per-activation frames; depth-counter fallback to frames on the fast path (see suspension). Dispatch: declared bound, default May. Open: the depth limit, and recursion through interfaces where the bound is the only information. Recommendation as written on those pages; test with a recursive-descent parser handler and a visitor over a tree.

docs.title: D6. Generics: monomorphisation or shared code
docs.text: Monomorphised: exact frames and effects, requires Tier B IR, code growth. Shared with dictionaries: no IR dependence, slower, hard to give generic frames a layout. Recommendation: monomorphise; revisit if code size hurts.

docs.title: D7. Can frame fusion work across separately compiled modules
docs.text: It can only when the callee's IR is present (Tier C) at link time. It cannot at module compile. If the callee's module ships A+B only, fusion simply does not happen across it. Alternative: export a fixed frame layout for chosen functions so callers can embed them without IR. This freezes the layout (breaking ABI to change). Recommendation: fusion at link time from IR only; no fixed layouts. Measure the benefit before building it: the toy numbers suggest about a nanosecond per call.

docs.title: D8. Debugging, stack traces and profiling
docs.text:
A parked task's native stack is gone; the logical stack is the frame chain. Fusion, lazy frames and inlining make logical frames not correspond to physical ones.

  • Park-point tables in every module (recommended): (frame type, state) -> chain of logical frames with source locations, as DWARF-style inline info. Tooling walks the frame chain for parked tasks, and the native stack plus the chain for running ones.
  • Profilers sample the native stack and append the chain. Needs a runtime hook.
  • Alternative: no maps; stack traces show only physical frames. Cheap, poor for diagnosing the "may park" chain which principle 10 demands tooling show.

docs.title: D9. Dynamic module loading and whole-program optimisation
docs.text: Aggressive devirtualisation and fusion assume a closed world; plugins break it. Alternatives: no dynamic loading; open interfaces declared in build configuration; a runtime flag that turns off closed-world assumptions entirely. Recommendation: no dynamic loading in the first compiler; keep bound-based dispatch so it can be added with open interfaces declared in configuration.

docs.title: D10. Blocking FFI
docs.text: Offload pool, dedicated thread, or run on worker. See the table in dispatch. Recommendation: nonblocking where possible; extern blocking offload by default; watchdog diagnostics.

docs.title: D11. Versioning module compatibility and native caches
docs.text: Format, ABI, contract hashes, cache keys as in modules. Open: whether the compatibility policy is enforced by the compiler (refuse a minor-version consumer of a major-breaking producer) or only reported; how long caches live; reproducible builds and cache portability across machines.

docs.title: D12. Cancellation as a non-exception
docs.text: Recommended: not in throws, not catchable, runs cleanups. Alternative: a catchable exception that must be rethrown. Interacts with the exception model (spec 10.7), and with child-vthread scopes.

docs.title: D13. Runaway non-parking code
docs.text:
Decided by the author: the compiler inserts budget checks in loops and recursion unless the function is tagged nopark. Mechanism in suspension 1.1.

Still open:

  • Overhead on tight loops. Unmeasured. Strip-mining and small-constant-bound elision are expected to keep it low; the number decides whether this stays the default. Benchmark B13.
  • Budget unit and source. An iteration counter (cheap, not time) against a timestamp (time, but needs a clock read or a flag set from another thread). Recommendation: counter, with the budget sized in iterations per check block, and a watchdog flag as a later addition for fairness across long checked regions.
  • Ripple. Most looping code becomes May. Library functions used inside sync/mutate, cleanups and C callbacks must be nopark; the standard library needs a deliberate pass. Recommendation: standard-library collections, copying, formatting and hashing are tagged nopark where their cost is bounded by a declared limit.
  • Where the check can be wrong. Unbounded nopark loops, plain extern fn, and large indivisible library operations still stall a worker. Recommendation: a lint on unbounded loops in nopark functions, and a watchdog diagnostic for workers that make no progress.
  • Interaction with fusion and the lazy shape. A check is a park point inside a loop, so the loop's live values must be spillable; a loop with borrowed locals falls under D2 too.

docs.title: 1. The may-park effect
docs.text:
Every function has an inferred effect summary. The part that matters for suspension is the park effect:

Park(f) = Never          f cannot park, on any path
        | May            f may park
        | Cond(P)        f parks only if an argument bound to a member of P may park
                         (P = function-typed parameters, interface-typed parameters, type parameters)

with the order Never < Cond(P) < May. The complete summary, which also records throws and foreign blocking, is in modules.

docs.title: Sources of parking
docs.text:
A function's own body can park only through these, and the analysis starts from them:

  1. A call to an extern parks fn (sleep, yield, waitAny, Conn.recv, Conn.send, ...). Already in stra/runtime/leaves.stra.
  2. Entering sync/mutate (it queues FIFO, see spec 7.1). The body of the block can never park, so a lock is never held across a suspension.
  3. A call to a function whose summary is May, or Cond(P) with a member of P bound to something that may park.
  4. A call through an interface or function value whose declared bound permits parking (see dispatch).
  5. A compiler-inserted budget check (Decided by the author; mechanism Direction). Every loop back-edge and every recursive call entry in a function not tagged nopark carries a check: decrement a per-worker budget, and when it is exhausted the task yields, which is an ordinary park point. This makes every function that contains a loop or recursion May, unless it is tagged nopark. See section 1.1.
  6. A call to a blocking foreign function that the runtime offloads (see blocking FFI).

Cleanup methods are Never by rule (spec section 9). A cleanup that tries to call a May function is a compile error, which is already the behaviour for sync/mutate bodies.

docs.title: Propagation
docs.text:
The effect propagates transitively over the call graph. Within a module it is computed as a fixed point over strongly connected components of the call graph:

for each SCC in reverse topological order:
    repeat until no change:
        for f in SCC:
            f.park = join(own park sources of f,
                          Park(g) for each direct callee g,    // imported g: read from its summary
                          bound(i) for each indirect call i)   // see dispatch

Mutually recursive functions share one SCC and end up with the same effect. A recursive function with no park source anywhere in its SCC stays Never.

Across modules the same computation runs on summaries (a few words per function) and never needs the callee's code. That is what lets an application be checked without anyone's source.

docs.title: Programmer-facing consequences
docs.text:
• No colouring in source. Nothing is written to opt in or out of parking. This is the one exception to principle 10 ("no hidden behaviour"), and it is unchanged.
  • Visibility is tooling's job (Decided, principle 10): hover, lints and errors that name the chain handle -> loadUser -> pool.acquire -> Conn.recv.
  • The nopark tag, written as an attribute on the function: fn[nopark] hash(key: u8[]&): u64. The opt-out is decided; the attribute spelling is the author's choice, with other details still open, see D4. A function written fn[nopark] ... is asserted Never: no budget checks are inserted in it, and the compiler rejects any park source in its body, including a call to a May function. It is not a colour: callers do not mention it and it is never required. It is the way to get plain C for a hot loop, and it turns a silent effect change into a compile error at a library boundary.

docs.title: 1.1 Budget checks and the nopark tag
docs.text:
The default is that code can be interrupted; opting out is explicit.

  • Where checks go: loop back-edges and recursive-call entries, not every function entry. A function with neither (straight-line code calling only Never functions) is inferred Never with no tag.
  • What a check is: a counter decrement and a rarely taken branch. When the budget runs out the task yields to the back of the run queue and resumes in its turn: a park point, so the live values are spilled to a frame exactly as for any park. Checks are also cancellation points, so a task in a long loop can be cancelled (CANCELLED wake, see section 4).
  • Cost control (Direction): strip-mine loops so the counter is tested once per block of iterations, not every iteration; omit the check for loops with a small constant bound. Neither is guaranteed; the overhead on tight loops must be measured (benchmarks B13).
  • Regions where a check is a park and so forbidden: the body of sync/mutate, cleanup methods, and callbacks entered from C. Code there is implicitly nopark, so a function called from them must be inferred or tagged nopark. Library functions likely to be used there (copying, hashing, sorting a small array, formatting) are the library author's to tag.
  • Consequence for the effect lattice: most application functions that loop are now May, so the May path is the common one and the per-call status test (about 0.7 to 1.5 ns, hand-written C, toy) applies broadly. The yields bit in the summary distinguishes "May only because of budget checks" from "can wait on I/O or a lock"; such a function never blocks on anything external.
  • Not a build option: checks are language semantics, so effect summaries are the same for every build and modules from different builds can be mixed. An experimental switch to disable checks exists only to measure their cost and stamps the module header; such modules do not link into a normal build.
  • Limits that remain: the budget bounds how long a checked region runs, not how long a nopark function, a plain extern fn, or a single indivisible library operation runs. A nopark function that loops without bound still stalls its worker, and that is now the author's explicit decision (tooling should warn on an unbounded loop in a nopark function).

docs.title: Example: checks, fn[nopark] and sync
docs.text:
Illustrative Strata source and the C a compiler might emit. Neither is compiler output.

// Loops and is not tagged: the compiler inserts a budget check. May, yields only.
fn parseHeaders(buf: u8[]&): Headers throws BadRequest {
    var h = Headers();
    var i = 0;
    while i < buf.len {              // back-edge: budget check inserted here
        let line = nextLine(buf, i);
        h.add(line);
        i = line.end;
    }
    return h;
}

// Hot, bounded, used under a lock: opt out. Plain C, no checks, may not park.
fn[nopark] hash(key: u8[]&): u64 {
    var x: u64 = 14695981039346656037;
    for b in key { x = (x ^ b) * 1099511628211; }   // no check
    return x;
}

fn lookup(cache: Ref<Cache>, key: u8[]&): i64? {
    let h = hash(key);               // Never: fine
    sync(cache) {                    // the body is implicitly nopark
        return cache.entries.get(h); // get() must be nopark, or this is a compile error
    }
}

fn[nopark] broken(k: u8[]&) {
    sleep(1ms);                      // error: park source in a nopark function
                                     //   broken -> sleep (extern parks)
}

Inferred effects:

hash          Never                 (tagged; no checks)
nextLine      Never                 (no loop, calls only Never functions)
parseHeaders  May, yields=true      (checks only; cannot wait on I/O or a lock)
lookup        May                   (acquiring the lock can park)

C for parseHeaders:

st_t parseHeaders_call(task_t *t, u8buf *buf, Headers *out) {
    Headers h = headers_new();
    size_t i = 0;
    while (i < buf->len) {
        if (--t->worker->budget <= 0) {              // budget check
            // a yield is a real park: spill live values into a frame
            parse_frame *f = frame_new(t, parseHeaders_resume, /*state*/ 1);
            f->buf = buf; f->h = h; f->i = i;        // buf is a borrowed parameter, see D2
            run_queue_push_back(t);
            return PARKED;
        }
        Line line = nextLine(buf, i);                // plain call
        headers_add(&h, line);
        i = line.end;
    }
    *out = h;
    return DONE;
}
// parseHeaders_resume re-enters the loop with f->h and f->i restored, or on CANCELLED
// runs the cleanups for h, frees the frame and returns CANCELLED.
  • hash has no counter and no status, so the C compiler can inline it freely.
  • On the common path a check costs a decrement and a branch per iteration. Strip-mining would test once per block. Neither cost nor strip-mining is measured yet (B13).
  • If buf pointed at a native-stack local in the caller, the caller would need a frame-resident local, or the yield would leave a dangling borrow (D2).
  • Library functions used inside sync/mutate (here entries.get) must be fn[nopark], so the standard library needs a deliberate tagging pass (D13).

docs.title: The three shapes of a function
docs.text:
Park(f) Generated form Never An ordinary C function. No frame, no status codes beyond throws. Cond(P) Compiled as two entries. A call whose P arguments are Never binds to the plain form; otherwise to the suspendable form. May The suspendable form below.

The key property for performance, and the reason conservatism is affordable: a May function that does not park on a given call costs about the same as an ordinary call. This was measured on the hand-written C (bench/results/lazy.md): about 0.7 to 1.5 ns per extra parking call in a chain, against ordinary calls, and 3.4 ns for the whole four-deep request. It is a microbenchmark with hot frames, so it supports "conservative contracts are cheap enough to be the default" and not much more.

docs.title: The suspendable form: native-stack fast path, frames made on demand (Direction)
docs.text:
Each May function is compiled to a pair:

f_call(task, args..., out*) -> status       runs on the worker's native stack
f_resume(task, frame*)      -> status       state-machine entry used after a park

status = DONE | THROWN | PARKED

f_call is the function as written, as straight C. Calls to other May functions check the returned status. If the callee returns PARKED, f_call does not park by itself. It allocates a frame, copies out the locals that are live across that call, records its state number, links the frame to the callee's frame, and returns PARKED to its own caller. The next function up does the same. A chain of N frames is therefore built from the leaf upward, during one return, and only when the park really happens.

When the event arrives, the scheduler calls the innermost frame's f_resume. When that finishes, it resumes its parent frame directly, in turn. This is the lazy strategy plus direct resume from the experiments. Two measured reasons it is the first choice:

  • Parks are rare relative to calls in typical handlers, so the common path allocates nothing (lazy.md: allocations per request = p x (D+1)).
  • Resuming only the innermost frame, rather than re-entering every frame from the root as Rust async does, kept wake cost flat with depth: 6.3 ns against 26.2 ns at depth 16 (bench/results/frames.txt).

The alternatives stay on the table because lazy needs two code versions per function that must agree on state numbering, and was 1.2x the code size of eager in the toy:

Strategy Allocations when no park Code When it wins Eager: a frame per May call D+1 smallest Frame-resident locals (below); debug builds Embedded: callee frames inside caller's frame 0 or 1 per task medium Chains that nearly always park (p near 1) Lazy: frames made while unwinding p x (D+1) largest Rare parks; default

The compiler may choose per function (Direction). The choice is invisible to callers because they only see status; that is what makes it a module-level decision and not an ABI one.

docs.title: Frame layout
docs.text:
A frame is:

+------------------------------+
| resume function pointer      |   header, identical for every function
| state number                 |   (the stable part of the ABI)
| parent frame link            |
| task pointer                 |
| result/out slot binding      |
+------------------------------+
| live slots                   |   private to the function
+------------------------------+

Live slots are the values live at some suspension point. Slots that are never live at the same time share storage, by the usual register-colouring over park points. Temporaries live across a park (an argument already evaluated for a call that has not happened, a pending Ref promotion) are slots like any others.

Frames come from a per-function arena, sized exactly. This matches the existing per-type arena rule and the frames_bench model; idle parked task cost there was 137 B with no state and 393 B at depth 4, against a 4 KB floor for a stackful fiber (Measured, hand-written).

Frames never move (Direction). A frame address is stable from creation to destruction. This removes the Pin problem Rust async has, and lets other code hold pointers into a frame.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
// module db (compiled separately)         Park(query) = May   (calls Conn.recv)
fn query(sql: string&, id: i64) -> Row throws DbError {
    let c = pool.acquire();                 // May: waits for a free connection
    c.send(encode(sql, id));                // May
    return decode(c.recv());                // May
}

// module app
fn handle(req: Request&) -> Response throws DbError {
    let row = db.query("select ...", req.id);   // inferred May; nothing written
    return render(row);                         // Never
}

Generated C for handle (illustrative; names and layout are not fixed):

typedef struct { frame_hdr h; Request *req; } handle_frame;   // row is not live across a park, so not a slot

st_t app_handle_call(task_t *t, Request *req, Response *out) {
    Row row;
    st_t s = db_query_call(t, "select ...", req->id, &row);
    if (s == PARKED) {                              // a real park, happening now
        handle_frame *f = frame_new(t, app_handle_resume, /*state*/ 1);
        f->req = req;
        t->innermost->parent = f;                   // link callee's frame to ours
        t->innermost->out = &f->h.result;           // the result now lands in the frame, not on our stack
        return PARKED;
    }
    if (s == THROWN) return THROWN;                 // no cleanups pending in this function
    *out = render(&row);                            // Never: a plain call
    return DONE;
}

st_t app_handle_resume(task_t *t, handle_frame *f) {
    switch (f->h.state) {
    case 1: {                                       // db.query finished
        if (t->wake == THROWN) { frame_free(f); return THROWN; }
        Response r = render((Row *)&f->h.result);
        frame_free(f);
        return finish(t, &r);                       // resume parent directly or complete the task
    }}
}

One real hazard shows in t->innermost->out = ...: the callee was given a pointer into the caller's native stack. Pointers to locals that are live across a park are the subject of the next subsection.

docs.title: Borrows and locals that cannot be moved
docs.text:
The lazy form copies locals into a frame only when a park occurs. A copy changes the address. Two things can hold the old address:

  1. A borrow (T&) to a local, given to a callee that is part of the park chain, or kept in another local.
  2. A result or out pointer (above), which the unwinding step can rebind because it is compiler-generated.

Case 2 is mechanical. Case 1 is not: let buf = readBuffer(); conn.recv(buf&) is exactly this shape, and extremely common.

Direction: a local that is borrowed and live across a call that may park is frame-resident from its declaration, in a frame created at function entry. A function with any frame-resident local uses the eager shape for that function. Other functions in the chain stay lazy. The borrow-origin analysis (spec section 5) already has what is needed to decide this; the new fact is only that the flag borrowed across a may-park call is recorded for each local. This is a real constraint on how often lazy applies, and not measured: the toy benchmark has no borrowed locals. See open decision D2.

docs.title: 3. Calls that never suspend
docs.text:
Never functions compile to ordinary C and are inlined by the C compiler under its usual rules. With budget checks on by default, a Never function is one that has no loop or recursion and calls only Never functions, or one tagged nopark. Parsing, rendering and hashing helpers that loop are May unless tagged, and the hot, bounded ones should be tagged. A Cond(P) function called with a known non-parking argument binds to its plain entry.

For a May function the non-suspending path should be straight-line C with one status test after each May call. The cost of that test is what the 0.7 to 1.5 ns above measures.

docs.title: Errors (throws)
docs.text:
C has no unwinding, so a throw is a status return (THROWN) with the exception in the task, and each function branches to its cleanup block for the scope it is in, then returns THROWN. This is the same machinery as the park return, which is why the two compose. Not built in the C prototypes yet (listed in open-questions.md).

Across a park, a thrown exception arriving at f_resume (t->wake == THROWN) enters the same cleanup blocks as it would on the fast path. The cleanup code is shared between f_call and f_resume; this is a code generation requirement, not a runtime one.

docs.title: Cancellation (Direction)
docs.text:
Cooperative, as in spec 6.2: the cancelling party marks the task and wakes it. A task is only ever cancelled at a park point, because that is where its state is in a frame. The wake carries wake = CANCELLED, and f_resume takes the unwinding path: run cleanups of the scopes it is in, free its own frame, resume the parent with CANCELLED, and so on up the chain. Frames are never discarded without running cleanups, and cleanups never park, so unwinding is bounded.

Cancellation is not an ordinary exception: it is not named in throws, and catch cannot swallow it. Letting catch (Exception) swallow it would make cancellation unreliable; requiring it in throws would put the effect back in signatures everywhere. This choice interacts with the open exception-model question (spec 10.7) and is stated here as Direction only.

A task can be cancelled at any park point, including a budget check, so a task spinning in a checked loop is cancellable. A task inside a nopark function, a plain extern fn or an indivisible library operation is not, until it returns.

docs.title: Deterministic cleanup
docs.text: Cleanup of a resource runs when its scope exits, by normal return, THROWN or CANCELLED, and happens before the frame is freed. Task-level cleanup precedes reclamation of any task arena (spec section 9, unchanged). A parked task holding a sync permission is impossible by construction (no park inside the block), so no frame ever owns a lock.

docs.title: 5. Recursion
docs.text:
• A recursive function with park sources in its SCC is May. Each activation has its own frame, taken from an arena, so recursion depth while parked is limited by memory, not by a stack size.
  • On the fast path a recursive May function consumes native stack until it returns or parks. A runaway recursion that never parks would overflow the worker's stack, as in any C program. Direction: a depth counter in recursive May functions; past a limit they switch to the eager shape (frames, not native stack), so depth is bounded by the declared limits (principle 11) rather than by the worker stack. Open: the limit, and whether recursive Never functions also need a declared depth bound.
  • Mutual recursion across modules is not possible through ordinary imports (module imports form a DAG). It can occur through interface calls, where the effect is the declared bound (see dispatch).

docs.title: 6. Interaction with ownership
docs.text: Concern Rule (Direction unless stated) Ref<T> live across a park Held in a frame slot; the slot is an owner. Frame destruction (normal, thrown or cancelled) releases it. A parked task therefore keeps its objects alive. WeakRef<T> live across a park Held in a slot. Promotion is a separate step after the resume, as everywhere (spec 3.1). The compiler must not hoist a promotion across a park point: the object may have expired meanwhile. Borrow T& live across a park Allowed if the referent outlives the parked task. The lifetime analysis (spec section 5) already tracks origins; the new check is that every referent a borrow can point to is either frame-resident, a Ref held by the frame, or static. A borrow of a native-stack local is the case handled above. Task temporary arena Belongs to the vthread, not to a frame. Survives parks. Reclaimed at task exit after cleanups. Per-function frame arenas Runtime-owned like per-type arenas. A frame can be freed on a different worker from the one that allocated it (a task can resume anywhere once migration exists), so frees must be cross-thread-safe; the same requirement as new. Escape analysis (spec 4.4) A value that does not escape the task may live in the task arena or in a frame slot. The compiler must preserve destructor timing across parks.

docs.title: 7. Optimisation opportunities
docs.text:
These are not guaranteed. Each is something the compiler may do when conditions hold, and none changes behaviour. The tier column says what each needs from the module format.

Opportunity What it is Conditions Needs Frame embedding The callee's slots live inside the caller's frame. One allocation per task instead of D+1. Callee frame size known; callee not recursive; one live activation per caller activation. Callee layout (link time, or a fixed layout exported from its module) Allocation elimination No frame for a function that never parks in practice Not provable; use lazy instead, which allocates only on a park None State-machine fusion Inline a May callee into its caller so its park points become states of the caller's machine; one frame, one resume function. Single call site, or small callee; direct (not virtual) target; not recursive. Callee IR (Tier C) Flattening A chain a -> b -> c becomes one machine The same, repeated; code size bounded Callee IR Slot overlay Slots from inlined callees share storage by liveness After fusion IR Direct resume Resume the innermost frame only Always applied by the lazy/direct scheme None Park-free specialisation A Cond(P) function called with a non-parking argument becomes Never Argument's effect known statically Summary

Limits on fusion: code size growth; an exported function still needs its own standalone entry points; debugging and profiling need a map from fused states back to logical frames (see open decisions D8); cancellation points and cleanup scopes of the inlined function must keep their order and timing exactly; recursion and virtual calls block it. The measured upper bound on what any of this can save is small in the toy case: about 1 ns per parking call, "a request that does any real work costs thousands of times more" (lazy.md). Fusion is therefore a later, evidence-driven optimisation, not part of the first compiler.

docs.title: 8. Relative to Java virtual threads and Rust async
docs.text:
Aspect Java virtual threads Rust async Strata (Direction) Source Plain blocking style async fn, .await, runtime choice Plain blocking style Suspension visible in signatures No Yes (async) No in source; yes in tooling and module summaries Implementation Stack of a continuation copied to and from the heap by the JVM (stackful) One compiler-generated state machine per async body, composed into a larger one Per-function resumable frames; compiler-generated Memory per parked task Depends on the stack depth at park, copied Size of the composed state machine, known statically Frames per function on the chain; exact, not yet measured in a compiler Can suspend through native frames Pinned or blocked in some cases (native, and synchronized on older JDKs) Not applicable: await only crosses async code No: foreign frames cannot be captured, so the rules in dispatch apply Runtime requirement JVM with JIT and GC Library executor Small C runtime, no GC, no JIT Dynamic code and reflection Natural Limited Weaker; closed-world assumptions help the optimiser Recursion Natural Needs boxing Natural (frames from arenas) dyn / virtual Natural Needs Box<dyn Future> and Pin Uniform: effect bound in the interface Cost of a function that might park but does not A call A poll, plus the state machine's size A call plus a status test (Measured, toy)

Advantages Strata is aiming for: no function colouring and no Pin; precise frames with no stack copying; deterministic cleanup on cancellation (Rust async cancels by dropping, Java by interrupts); no runtime beyond the C one.

Trade-offs and limitations, stated plainly:

  • Every function the analysis marks May costs a status test per May call and extra generated code. The analysis can mark a function May because of a deep, unseen callee; nothing in the source says so.
  • Compile-time complexity moves from the programmer to the compiler: effect inference, frame layout, two code versions per function, and a module format that must carry it all.
  • Foreign code cannot be suspended in the middle. Java's pinning problem exists here in a different form (see dispatch).
  • Stack traces and profilers see the native stack, not the logical one, unless the toolchain supplies maps.
  • No performance superiority is claimed. The existing measurements are small, hand-written, and mostly show a memory advantage over stackful fibers (and parity with Tokio-class frames). See the evaluation plan.

docs.title: 9. Where stackful execution remains
docs.text:
1. As the reference semantics. The tests that decide whether a language feature is correct should pass under both implementations, which is cheap to arrange if the stackful runtime is kept working.
  2. As a baseline for the evaluation plan: stackful fibers are the cost to beat on memory (4 KB floor, 4.1 KB resident at 1 KB state against Tokio's 1.4 KB).
  3. For synchronous drivers on blocking-pool threads, where a foreign callback needs to call parking Strata code (dispatch).

It is no longer the primary implementation path. Spec section 6.1 is rewritten accordingly.

docs.title: The journey
docs.text:
Step Question Answer in one line 1. Why Strata What does Goose leave out for servers? Dynamic objects, shared state and many lightweight threads. 2. Foundations What do fibers, arenas, refcounts and frames cost? A 4 KB fiber floor, free arena layout choices, no biased counts, about 1 ns per parking call. 3. An HTTP server Can the model carry a real server? Yes: 88 to 94 B per idle connection, throughput syscall-bound. 4. Rust and Go Is it any better than what exists? Memory per connection, yes; pipelined throughput, about 2x; real handlers shrink the gap. 5. mini-redis What does a second, different server break? Cross-worker wakeups, pub/sub backpressure, a shared database. 6. Locks that park How should sync and mutate wait? Park in FIFO order, spin briefly first, acquire several locks all-or-nothing.

All numbers were measured on one machine (Ryzen 9 9950X3D, Linux 6.12, gcc 14.2, rustc 1.93, Go 1.24, OpenJDK 25), usually from single runs. Raw data lives in bench/results/.

docs.title: 1. Why Strata
docs.text:
Goose offers compiler-managed lifetimes, native C output and large virtual-memory reservations that let selected arrays grow in place. Its strict thread isolation and limited dynamic allocation make typical server programs awkward.

Strata keeps those ideas and adds what a server needs:

  • dynamically created objects and graphs with independent lifetimes
  • thousands of virtual threads running ordinary sequential code
  • efficient shared, read-heavy state such as caches
  • deterministic cleanup of files, sockets and locks
  • reference safety without writing lifetime names like 'a

It is not a Goose fork or a Rust dialect, and it does not try for feature parity with Rust. Understandable semantics win over zero overhead at all costs.

docs.title: The first rules
docs.text:
Two rules shaped everything after them, and both came from the user rather than from measurement:

Principle 10: no hidden magic

Aside from virtual threads and parking, nothing happens behind the programmer's back. No implicit buffering, no implicit batching. A library may offer batching, but only when the program asks for it, and it is off by default.

Principle 11: every unbounded input has a limit

A header block, a request body and a parsed document's depth all have limits stated by the program. Big payloads are streamed or spooled to a file, never parsed whole. Exceeding a limit is an error the caller can see.

docs.title: 2. Measuring the foundations
docs.text: Before writing any Strata, the expensive questions got small C benchmarks, compared with Rust (Tokio, slab) and Java virtual threads where one existed. Full tables: group1.md, group2.md, group56.md, lazy.md.

docs.title: Fibers and stacks
docs.text:
Unit (100k idle, 1 KB state) Resident bytes each Tokio task 1,419 (395 with no state) Strata pooled-stack fiber 4,113 (one page floor) Java virtual thread about 809 heap with no state
  • A stackful fiber has a 4 KB floor; a stackless task is about 10x smaller when idle state is small. The gap closes near page size.
  • MADV_NOHUGEPAGE is mandatory with transparent huge pages on: without it a 64 KB stack costs 65 KB resident, and a 1 MB stack almost 1 MB.
  • Per-stack guard pages do not scale: each costs two mappings, and 1M fibers hit the map-count limit.
  • Switching is cheap: about 13 ns with 1k fibers, 35 to 39 ns with 100k.

docs.title: Typed arenas
docs.text:
• Layout (one reservation, a chunk table, or munmap) makes no measurable difference to allocation cost; choose by what handles need.
  • Smaller chunks reclaim better, and geometric growth removes the small-type floor.
  • Against glibc, after freeing everything an arena returns memory (0.3 MB retained against 153 MB).
  • MADV_DONTNEED zero-fills, so a generation stored in a slot is lost when a chunk is decommitted. The fix is a per-chunk epoch kept in the resident chunk header.
  • Long-lived objects scattered through shared chunks pin memory. That is solved by lifetime segregation, which per-type arenas give by construction.

docs.title: Reference counts across threads
docs.text:
• Biased counting is 2 to 7x cheaper than atomic for thread-private objects, but once objects cross threads it is equal or worse (0.71 to 0.87x at 16 threads with message passing).
  • Decision: no biased counting in v1. Types proven thread-confined get plain counts; shared types get plain atomic counts.
  • Messaging stays for passing data, with typed per-vthread mailboxes. Shared memory with sync and mutate is the primary sharing model.

docs.title: Frames for parked calls
docs.text:
Four strategies were compared: plain calls, a heap frame per call (eager), frames embedded in the caller, and lazy frames created only while unwinding a real park.

  • Lazy beats eager by 3.6 ns per request at depth 4 and 7.7 ns at depth 8 when parks are rare. The whole difference between strategies is about 1 ns per parking call.
  • An earlier estimate of 20 to 30 ns saved per request was too high; the measured saving is 4 to 8 ns.
  • Parked memory is the same for lazy and eager.

docs.title: 3. An HTTP server
docs.text: The first proving ground. The server is written as .stra source, with a hand-written C counterpart standing in for compiler output. Tests pin the two together.

docs.title: What it showed
docs.text:
4 workers, 64 active connections per idle connection requests/s Strata-style C, 100k connections 89 B 1.29M Tokio, lazy futures 897 B 1.25M Tokio, naive handler 3,074 B 1.25M
  • The 88 B is sizeof(ConnTask) and nothing else: an idle connection holds no buffer.
  • Throughput is nearly equal because the workload is syscall-bound (about 3 microseconds per request). The frame model buys memory, not a large throughput win.
  • Kernel memory (3 to 3.6 KB per socket) dwarfs all of it and is the same for every server.

docs.title: Features that were added, each from a review
docs.text:
• Size-class input buffers replaced a fixed 2 KB buffer; the reader no longer moves bytes per request.
  • Two body readers: a small in-memory one for APIs (1 MB default) and a file-backed upload reader with a much larger limit. Both refuse an oversize body with 413 before holding it.
  • Pipelined requests run as one child task each, answered in request order, with a barrier for unsafe methods.
  • Opt-in response batching, off by default, with a bound on held responses and a max hold time. It exists to honour principle 10.
  • Lingering close, so an error response is not destroyed by a reset when the client is still sending.
  • Layering: generic support moved into runtime and library files; server.stra holds only the server.

docs.title: Negative controls
docs.text: Each important property has a build that breaks it on purpose (responses in completion order, no body limits, no yield, and so on), and the matching test must fail. 38 tests pass and every control fails as intended.

docs.title: 4. Against Rust and Go
docs.text:
The same design was written in Rust (Tokio) and Go (a pipelined server, and plain net/http), driven by the same tests and load generator.

Pipelined, 1 worker requests/s Strata-style C 4.05M Rust (Tokio) 2.1M Go 2.12M Idle memory per connection bytes Strata-style C 89 to 192 Rust about 1,400 Go 4,000 to 5,000 Go net/http 33,000

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
Caveats

Real handlers do real work, which shrinks the throughput gap a lot. What survives is memory per connection, in-connection concurrency, the timer floor and Go's garbage-collection tail. All runs are single runs on loopback.

Browsers do not pipeline HTTP/1.1 (they multiplex over HTTP/2), so the pipelined number says more about the runtime's cost per request than about web traffic.

docs.title: 5. mini-redis
docs.text:
The second proving ground, chosen because it differs from HTTP: long-lived connections, pub/sub fan-out and one shared database. The server side of tokio-rs/mini-redis was converted (frame, parse, connection, db, server, shutdown, commands).

Conversion depends on no third-party crates

If a program needs a crate, Strata would have no equivalent. The README maps each crate used by the original to a replacement, and lists the standard-library pieces the Strata source assumes.

docs.title: What was new
docs.text:
• Cross-worker wakeups: a publish on one worker must wake a subscriber parked on another.
  • Backpressure: one mailbox per subscriber connection with a declared capacity and an explicit lag policy, Disconnect (default) or Notice.
  • A reaper: cleanup() cannot take a lock, so a dying subscriber hands its subscriptions to a queue, and a purge vthread unsubscribes them.
  • Fairness: a pipelining publisher starved subscribers until each connection yielded every 64 commands.
  • Limits everywhere: frame size, bulk size, key length, key count, topics, subscriptions and queue depth.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Item Result GET/SET 90/10, 1 worker 328k ops/s unpipelined, 468k pipelined 16 deep 4 workers 1.10M to 1.94M; the load generator tops out near 1.3M unpipelined Pub/sub deliveries, 1 / 4 workers 440 to 456k/s / up to 1.98M/s Median delivery latency, 1 worker 12 µs for 1 subscriber, 84 µs for 64, 1.4 ms for 1,000 Idle connection / idle subscriber 297 B / 354 to 594 B

The idle subscriber first cost 4.5 KB because the mailbox ring was allocated at full size; growing it on demand fixed that.

docs.title: Tests and honesty
docs.text:
27 tests pass on six builds (plain, park-only, and both under AddressSanitizer and ThreadSanitizer), with four negative controls. Bugs found along the way included a wake sent to an uninitialised worker and two data races, fixed.

There is no baseline: building the original Rust server was blocked by the permission system, so none of these numbers is compared with Rust.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
Entering sync or mutate may park the virtual thread. A holder never parks inside the block (a compile error), so two vthreads on one worker never contend and hold time is bounded by the code in the block.

Several objects in one head, as in mutate(a, b), are acquired all-or-nothing in a fixed global order; if one is busy the acquirer releases everything, parks on that lock's FIFO queue and retries, keeping its arrival ticket. Nested acquisition of another object, reentrancy and read-to-write upgrade are errors.

docs.title: The ordering key
docs.text: The order is by the address of each object's lock word, or (arena id, slot index) for arena objects whose storage can move. A per-allocation sequence number was rejected for its cost. Arenas never compact, and a chunk is freed only when empty, so a live object's address never changes. Only types that appear in a sync or mutate head carry a lock word.

docs.title: The measurement that changed the contract's implementation
docs.text:
With FIFO fairness, one waiting writer makes every later reader queue behind it, and each handoff is a cross-thread wake. Throughput at 4 workers, one lock, 64 connections:

GET share park only spin then park 100% 1.29M 1.29M 90% 570k 1.28M 50% 330k 1.27M 0% 318k 1.27M

A 10% write mix lost 55% of throughput. Spinning 2000 rounds before parking removed the loss. The contract is unchanged (entering still "may park"); only the cost differs. A 100-round spin was noisy, from 1.0M to 326k at 50% reads.

The park-only build remains in the test suite so the handoff path stays covered.

Not yet implemented

The multi-object retry exists only as design. mini-redis has a single lock.
